claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNiTi powder is equiatomic.
Conventional casting of CoCrFeNiTi produces porosity.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has a soft, single-phase FCC structure.
The cast baseline has a hardness of approximately 200 HV and low strength.
High-energy ball milling followed by rapid sintering will suppress porosity in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed process will produce a nanocrystalline solid solution dominated by FCC with minor BCC while suppressing HCP.
High-energy milling at 300–500 rpm for 10–20 hours is an appropriate operating range.
Rapid sintering at 800–1000°C for less than 10 minutes under 50–100 MPa in Ar is an appropriate densification regime.
A sintering strain rate of 10^-2 to 10^-1 s^-1 maximizes FCC/BCC dual-phase stability.
Keeping displacement rate below 10 nm/s prevents excessive grain growth.
Heating and cooling rates above 100°C/min manage thermal-expansion mismatch and minimize residual stress.
The processed alloy will have a grain size below 100 nm.
High-energy milling introduces a high defect density and reduces particle size, thereby promoting solid-solution formation.
Rapid sintering suppresses HCP nucleation by limiting the time available for Ti-rich segregation and phase transformation.
At intermediate temperatures, entropy-driven mixing dominates enthalpy-driven ordering and maximizes FCC/BCC stability.
The processed material will have less than 1% porosity.
Hardness will increase by 50–100% relative to the cast material.
Yield strength will exceed 600 MPa.
Ductility will remain above 10% elongation.
Ti contents above 25 at% lead to HCP dominance.

contradictions.description: The initial alloy is stated to be equiatomic, which places Ti at 20 at%, but the stated applicability boundary requires Ti content below 20 at%; the proposed starting composition therefore lies outside the declared applicable range.

The mechanism attributes increased hardness jointly to grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening, whereas the requested causal claim and proposed test frame grain refinement as an alternative to solute strengthening. A single hardness threshold cannot distinguish these contributions.
